rules.statement: Every shooter stage exists twice with the same name, tunable names and math: as a class registered in ShooterStages.java and as an entry in the DEFS object of TeamCode/sim/shooter-brain-testbed.html. A stage added or changed in one place is added or changed in the other in the same change.
Pipeline stages (RangeFilter, VelocityModifier, FireGate) touch no hardware, no HardwareMap, no clock and never sleep; everything they need arrives in RangeFrame or ShotContext.

The pipeline spec string (ShooterConfig.PIPELINE) is the only hand-off between the sim and the robot; Pipeline.fromSpec(Pipeline.toSpec(p)) must reproduce p, and a spec the sim exports must parse on the robot.
ShooterBrain, Pipeline, CalibrationTable and the stages import nothing from com.qualcomm or org.firstinspires so they run under plain JUnit on a laptop.
The brain never reports fire=true before a goal tag has been observed, and a stage returning NaN, infinity or a negative value is ignored rather than propagated into the flywheel target.
A Limelight result that has not changed since the last poll is not fed to the brain again; duplicated frames would bias every rolling filter.

optOut.reason: The copy in this repository is teaching material: a kickoff deck (docs/kickoff-deck) and a classroom simulator (TeamCode/sim). Its job is to explain how the shooter works, so a rule that forbids explanatory prose forbids the material.

Teaching copy repeats a term on purpose (glossary, then use) and shows worked examples; the product-copy brevity rule would strip the scaffolding first-year students need. Concision is still checked by COPY-TEACH-CONCISE.
A stage description that says what a stage fixes and what it costs is the lesson; students are asked to write exactly that sentence in the challenge.
The deck's closing section is a plan by design: it tells students what to do before calibration night.

rules.statement: Every number, file name, command, tag ID, stage name and test count in teaching copy matches the repository as it stands (README.md in the shooter package, ShooterStages.java, ShooterConfig.java, ShooterBrainTest.java, parity-vectors.txt). A finding wherever one is stale, rounded up or invented.

A technical term in the deck is given a plain-words meaning on the slide where it first appears, or on a glossary slide that comes earlier in deck.json order. A finding wherever a first-year student would meet a term before its meaning.
A reader who knows nothing about shooters follows each slide or sim panel on one read: one idea per slide, sentences under about twenty-five words, no sentence that needs the next one to make sense.

Nothing is said twice within a slide or panel, and no sentence is filler (an opener that announces the topic, a closer that restates it). Repetition across slides is allowed when the second use is a glossary term being applied.

Teaching copy sounds like a mentor talking to this team: direct address, concrete nouns from this robot and this field, no marketing register, no exclamation, no rhetorical question answered in the next line.
Each section of the deck (deck.json sections) ends with something the student does, not only something they now know.
